samples.question: The cream board carries six square tiles that never touch each other, plus small pale decorative squares lying on the bare board that mean nothing. Every tile is a 5 by 5 grid of cells inside a thick coloured frame. A cell is either FILLED, showing a small dark square, or EMPTY, showing plain white, or COVERED, showing a flat grey block that hides the whole cell. Exactly two tiles wear the same dark slate-grey frame: these are the two VIEWS, and they sit at opposite corners of the board, far apart. Both views show the very same hidden 5 by 5 pattern, cell for cell, in the same orientation, without any rotation or reflection; the only difference between them is which cells their grey covers hide. The two views never cover the same cell, so a cell hidden in one view is always shown in the other, and putting the two views together reveals the whole hidden pattern. The other four tiles are the CANDIDATES. Each candidate wears a frame in a different colour taken from red, orange, green, teal, blue and purple, and no candidate has any grey cover: all twenty-five of its cells are visible. Exactly one candidate matches the hidden pattern in every one of its twenty-five cells. Every candidate has exactly the same number of filled cells, so the amount of dark ink, the number of filled cells, the frame colour, the tile size and the tile position tell you nothing about which one is right. Each wrong candidate was made from the hidden pattern by turning some filled cells empty and the same number of empty cells filled. At least one wrong candidate agrees with everything the first view shows, and at least one wrong candidate agrees with everything the second view shows, so reading only one view can never decide the answer: you must combine what both distant views reveal and then compare that fused pattern with the four candidates. Which candidate matches the hidden pattern? Give the colour of that candidate's frame. Answer red, orange, green, teal, blue or purple.
